claim: Re-expressing a Bayes problem as natural (absolute) frequencies raises correct answers, but most people still fail even then (16% to 46% Bayesian algorithms; 20% to 36% correct; meta-analysis 4% to 24%).
agent_test: Same base-rate item set: probability wording vs agent first rewriting to counts out of N (O6), answer by code; compare accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: The frequency benefit is not universal: it depends on numeracy and person; person-level differences explain far more variance than format (marginal R2 .065 vs conditional .685). At fixed menu the format gap is still 22 to 30 points in humans, but the short menu alone lifts probability-format answers from 16% to 28% (d07).
agent_test: Check whether the count rewrite helps only on problems where the plain model first fails; route only those.

claim: Relative frequencies (percent) do not help; only absolute counts that carry the base rate do (60 vs 66 Bayesian solutions, counts, Study 2).
agent_test: Compare percent rewrite vs count rewrite vs raw probabilities.

claim: Best fix for base-rate problems is to extract the numbers and compute the posterior in code, not to rely on prose reasoning.
agent_test: Arm: model extracts prior, hit rate and false-alarm rate into JSON; code applies Bayes. Versus plain CoT and versus a natural-frequency prompt. No source tested this exact arm. Indirect support only: a code interpreter nearly closed the counting gap in Pournemat et al. (d13); instructions alone did not fix judgment biases (d12).

claim: Models told to use a natural-frequency strategy follow it only some of the time and can still end wrong; telling them to apply Bayes' rule did not change similarity-driven answers until the most forceful prompt.
agent_test: Measure compliance: does the trace contain the counts, and does code reproduce the answer. b24 and c22 are the same author, so treat as about 1.5 sources.

claim: LLMs act Bayesian on uncharacteristic descriptions but largely ignore the base rate when the description is stereotypical; they recall base rates inconsistently (2-4% asked directly, 10-30% inside a posterior judgment).
agent_test: Force the agent to state the base rate in a separate call before seeing the description, then combine in code.

claim: The conjunction fallacy is robust in humans: 83-92% violate in direct rank tests and it persists under betting and hidden-sentence controls, so it is not only a wording artefact.
agent_test: Nothing to install for humans; for the agent see K08 and K09.

claim: Frequency wording and explicit inclusion cues reduce but do not remove the conjunction error (65% to 25% in the heart-attack survey); the polysemy account (Hertwig and Gigerenzer) is only partly supported by betting controls.
agent_test: Rewrite probability questions as 'how many of 100' and compare.

claim: Strong LLMs pass the classic Linda item; on freshly written Linda-form items GPT-4 also passed in 2023 (.98), but name and token perturbations and flipped-logic versions still catch 2024-25 models, so the pass is partly pattern matching, not only memorisation.
agent_test: Run paired original vs mutated items: new names, irrelevant tokens, and a flipped-logic version where the conjunction is the right answer (G3). Fresh surface alone is not a strong enough mutation (d09).

claim: Replacing bias-triggering words with meaningless tokens cut the conjunction error in chatbots (0/20 to 10/10 in one item).
agent_test: Strip content words, answer by structure, compare with original; tiny N, replicate before use.

claim: Category-based induction in humans shows a stable cluster of effects: similarity, typicality, specificity, sample size, premise diversity, with boundaries (young children, Itzaj Maya, non-monotonicity).
agent_test: Use as a checklist of premise features when the agent generalises from cases.

claim: Similarity alone is the wrong default for non-blank properties; people prefer causal-structure inference over shared-attribute inference (13/16 and 14/16 participants).
agent_test: Agent names the structure (taxonomy, causal link, threshold) before generalising; compare with a similarity-only prompt.

claim: Structured Bayesian models fit human property induction (r .85 to .96 for tree plus diffusion) and explain diversity and typicality that single similarity sums cannot.
agent_test: Fits are to averaged ratings, hand-chosen structures; a02, a05, a06, a30 share the Kemp/Tenenbaum lab. Not a testable agent mechanism.

claim: GPT-4 reproduces most classic induction phenomena but fails specific non-monotonicity (a dissimilar extra premise should weaken the argument; it strengthens it); GPT-3.5 depends on argument order.
agent_test: All six lines are one paper (Han et al.). Run non-monotonicity items with a note on why premises were chosen; check the effect.

claim: Hypothesis search (propose rules in language, write each as code, run on examples) beats direct answering: ARC 17% to 30% (GPT-4, 100 tasks), 1D-ARC 39.6% to 73.1%, List Functions 31% to 69%.
agent_test: All lines are one paper (Wang et al.); c12 and c13 give related program-search results. Replicate on our ARC portfolio at equal tokens versus best-of-N.

claim: The bottleneck in hypothesis search is choosing the right hypothesis, not coding it: a correct one was in the pool for 49 of 100 tasks; human selection gave 33%, model summary 30%. A second study (GPT-4o, 100 list functions) found the model's own summarising step drops 26% of correct hypotheses, while running code on the examples rescued 37% of trials where the front end failed (d01, d02).
agent_test: Keep the whole pool; rank by code run on the examples. Measure pool-contains-correct vs chosen-correct on our tasks. Not tested: held-out example vs agreement vs size prior.

claim: Language models propose good rules but cannot reliably apply their own rules; a symbolic interpreter that runs rules raises accuracy (ACRE 28 to 45-59, MiniSCAN 0 to 46, List Functions 39.6 to 52).
agent_test: Execute proposed rules in code on every example. b20 and c06-c09 are one paper (Qiu et al.).

claim: Iterative refinement mostly patches failures with exceptions and can hurt on hard tasks (MiniARC 13.8 plain vs 3.8 at T=1,N=1 and 14.6 at T=3,N=5, no real gain); execution feedback gains plateau after about 2 rounds on ARC.
agent_test: Cap refinement rounds at 2; compare with fresh resampling.

claim: Noise in examples, even one bad example, degrades LLM induction substantially. Subset sampling plus code execution (SRR) kept accuracy within about 2 points at 10% noise (d16).
agent_test: Inject one wrong example and see whether a held-out check lets the agent detect the outlier.

claim: Brute-force sampling of programs filtered by training examples scales about +3 points per doubling of samples on ARC (GPT-4o, about 8,000 samples per problem, 50% on the public test set).
agent_test: Plot accuracy vs samples at fixed total tokens; compare uniform vs difficulty-based allocation.

claim: Induction (program synthesis) and transduction (direct prediction) solve different ARC tasks; ensembling gave 26.5% vs 18.8% and 15.3%.
agent_test: Run both routes; select by agreement with a held-out example. Their models were trained, ours is a scaffold.

claim: Programs that fit all train examples still fail the test: about 9% in Li et al. (2024) on their tasks, but 28.7% of first attempts by o3-mini on 1114 general functions fit all 10 examples and fail a differential-testing oracle (d06). The rate depends on how well the examples pin the function down.
agent_test: Hold one example out for every induced rule and also generate new inputs and compare candidate rules on them; held-out alone will miss under-specification.

claim: In the number game a reasoning model stays anchored to the shown number after one example and is best fit by likelihood without a prior, while an LLM-proposal plus Bayesian weighting reproduces human curves; whether an explicit candidate list fixes it is not settled.
agent_test: Probe one-example generalisation; test an explicit candidate-hypothesis list prompt. New: Bazigaran and Sohn confirm anchoring on one example (d05); a weak-sampling prompt and thinking mode shift toward the prior but do not remove narrowness (d04). Candidate-list prompt still untested.

claim: Proposing hypotheses with an LLM and weighing them by a prior and likelihood in code reproduces human number-game curves with 50 to 100 proposals.
agent_test: Implement propose-then-weigh in code for rule-induction tasks; N=8 humans in the source.

claim: Debiasing prompts help response biases but can backfire for judgment biases; instructions to avoid the bias are unreliable.
agent_test: Compare any avoid-bias prompt against plain at equal tokens; keep only if it wins.

claim: Most LLM errors on classic heuristics tasks are illogical rather than human-like biased (GPT-4 69.2% correct with correct reasoning).
agent_test: b23 and c20 are the same paper listed twice. Inspect real failures rather than assuming human-bias fixes apply.

claim: Recalibrating probability forecasts with one power parameter on log odds cut Brier score by about 45% to 62%, mostly near term; extremizing sometimes helps, sometimes hurts. For LLM forecasts, two-parameter Platt scaling cut Brier on four models (Claude-Sonnet-4 .146 to .129; trained on 7,824 questions) but Brier gains from ECE-only fixes can be an illusion (d14, d15).
agent_test: Collect agent confidences with outcomes; fit slope and intercept in code on held-out items; accept only if Brier (not just ECE) falls. Minimum sample size still unknown.

claim: LLMs update beliefs poorly over repeated interaction; tuning toward a Bayesian assistant improved agreement to about 80%.
agent_test: Relevant only if the agent accumulates evidence across turns; training is outside our no-training scope.

claim: Between a model-written shortlist and the full candidate pool, the shortlist step loses good hypotheses: the GPT-4o summariser dropped 26% of correct hypotheses (generator 46.4% correct, after summarising 34.5%).
agent_test: Rank the full pool by running code on the examples; compare against a model-written shortlist at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs judge a shown list of hypotheses better than they author the best hypothesis: evaluation picked hypotheses that fit the examples better than free generation did, which favoured narrow rule-like ones.
agent_test: After generating candidates, give the model the list and ask it to score each against all examples; compare with taking its first free answer.

claim: In humans the frequency format helps even when the menu is held fixed (46% vs 16% standard menu, 50% vs 28% short menu), but the menu of joint counts alone explains part of the gain; no LLM study crosses format and menu.
agent_test: Four-arm test on base-rate items: probability or frequency wording crossed with standard or short menu, with and without code.

claim: The frequency benefit in the Linda problem may come from providing a concrete reference class and nested sets, not from frequency wording: with that confound removed, frequency and probability formats did equally well.
agent_test: Rewrite conjunction items to name the reference class ('of 100 women like Linda') and compare with a pure frequency wording.

claim: A prompt that tells the model to avoid bias does not reliably help judgment biases and can slightly worsen them (-4.4% accuracy) while fixing response biases (+40.5%).
agent_test: Do not use a bare avoid-the-bias instruction on probability items; use computation or a checked rewrite.

claim: Prose reasoning loses count of frequencies as context grows and does worse on conditional than joint distributions; letting a model write code to count nearly restores accuracy (GPT-4.1-mini).
agent_test: Route any conditional-probability step with more than a few counts to code.

claim: Rule induction under noisy examples is helped by sampling diverse subsets of the examples and verifying rules by code, without needing to find the bad example.
agent_test: Induce on random subsets, keep the rule fitting the most examples, flag the examples it misses.

claim: No source tests whether naming a taxonomy or causal structure in the prompt improves LLM property induction, nor whether a teacher-assumption prompt repairs non-monotonicity in current models.
agent_test: In-house arm: similarity-only prompt vs prompt that first names taxonomy or causal link, equal tokens, on blank-property arguments.
